newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FORECAST-PLDT H1 net seen slightly higher.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-PLDT H1 net seen slightly higher.

text.p: The Philippines' largest telephone company could see slightly higher profits for the first half of the year despite redundancy expenses and delays in introducing a new tariff structure, analysts said on Tuesday.

A Reuters poll of eight brokerage houses, four of whom predicted the first half results, showed the Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co's (PLDT) net income from January to June was expected to increase by 9.28 percent to 3.18 billion pesos.
For the first half of 1996, PLDT registered 2.91 billion pesos in profits. Full year 1996 income was 6.44 billion pesos.

"There will be a redundancy charge although we do not know how much PLDT will book for the first half, but operation-wise, there will be a 20 percent growth in recurring earnings for the first half," Louie Hilado, analyst at ING Baring Securities, said.
PLDT's profits dropped 1.8 percent to 1.28 billion pesos in the first quarter of the year as the company paid 251.8 million pesos in a separation package to 3,000 employees.
Hilado said PLDT's revenues in the first half of the year from domestic calls was expected to grow by 30 percent although international revenue growth rate could be flat.
"Local revenue growth is fast catching up with international revenues and PLDT is on schedule in terms of installation of lines," Alexis Cabel, analyst at Angping Securities, said.

Orion Squire-Capital Inc research head Cilette Liboro said international revenues would still make up bulk of the revenues at 52 percent, local call revenues, 31 percent and national long distance revenues, 17 percent.

"People should look at operating income to see that for the year, there will actually be growth for PLDT. For 1997, we expect operating revenues at 32.37 billion pesos from last year's 28.66 billion," Liboro said.
Analysts said a number of issues were yet to be resolved to be able to determine with more certainty PLDT's financial performance for the year.

The accounting rates have yet to be settled. The United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has been pushing for a drastic reduction in the cost of international calls over the next two years. PLDT has been pushing for a more gradual reduction.
PLDT and its U.S. counterparts are yet to finalise a rate. Analysts had assumed a 15 to 20 percent cut for the year.

Secondly, PLDT is yet to secure the approval of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) for a rate restructuring that will help the carrier meet increasing competition and compensate for the lower accounting rates from international calls.
Most analysts said PLDT's income could pick up in the second half once its rate restructuring petition was accepted.
PLDT wants to raise basic phone charges and introduce a metering system for local calls. The NTC could try and temper the rise in local charges, analysts said.
"We expect a watered down version and it may take a while for PLDT to implement a metering scheme," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities.
Despite uncertainties over rates and growing competition, PLDT was expected to hold on to its market share.
"It would take a while before competitors close in on PLDT and the pie is also getting bigger," said Mejia.
